generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up in how a session is run in any subject: a seminar built around a task you complete, a workshop that asks you to apply or evaluate rather than only listen. Tutors plan these from the outcomes they want you to reach, so the activity in the room is there for you to do. Reading what a session is designed to make you do, then preparing for that, is how you get the most from it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students with the same workshop on their timetable. It is built around a task to complete, with a pre-task: read one short piece and come ready to use it.

Student A reads the piece and highlights the main points to remember later. In the workshop, Student A waits to be told what it all means. The session was built around doing something with the reading, but Student A prepared as if it were a lecture, so there is little to offer. This treats an active design as a passive one.

Student B notices the pre-task is asking for something to be used, not just recalled, and prepares for that: a point to make, and a reason behind it. In the workshop, Student B joins the task straight away. By reading what the session was designed to do, Student B arrived ready to do it.

Both students did the reading. Only Student B worked out what the session was designed to make them do, and prepared for that.
generatedProse.summary: University learning is designed to be active: you learn by doing the thing, not by watching it done. Most of it is built so you construct understanding through activity, with some step-by-step training where a skill needs practice. Tutors plan backwards from the outcomes they want, so each activity has a purpose you can see. You can now tell an active design from a passive one, explain why outcomes come first, and work out how to engage with a session on its own terms. The next lesson turns to how your work is judged.

check.body: A tutor sets the outcome 'by the end you will be able to evaluate an argument' before planning the session. Why decide the outcome first?

items.text: So the activities and content can be built to lead you to that outcome (constructive alignment).
Because the outcome is a formality recorded after the class.
So the session can cover as much material as possible.
Because the reading must be chosen before anyone knows its purpose.

feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding the outcome first lets the tutor align the session's activities and reading to it, which is constructive alignment.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the outcome is for in the design of the session.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The outcome is set first so the activities and reading can be aligned to lead you to it. This backward design is constructive alignment.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
